column4: The ayah's emphatic pouring of water is the first exact step in the section's field sequence: the field and the soul receive growth from above.
The earth is explicitly split open, matching both the section's ploughing sense of falaha and its water-opening sense of fajara.
Grain is made to grow from the opened earth, completing the section's water-splitting-growth sequence and making zakkaha perceptible as cultivation.
Good land yields vegetation by its Lord's permission while bad land yields only stunted growth; this is the section's two souls as fertile field and barren ground in one ayah.
Rain strips the thin soil from a smooth rock, showing exactly how the same water that nourishes a true field exposes ground incapable of growth.
Rain makes a high garden yield twice its fruit, directly staging the section's divinely blessed growth and contrasting the rock of 2:264.
Allah causes human beings to grow from the earth as a plant; this directly grounds the section's reading of cultivating the nafs as cultivating a field.
Salih tells Thamud that Allah produced them from the earth and settled them to cultivate it, identifying the camel-killers as a people raised in productive land.
Thamud's gardens and springs supply the fertile, watered setting in which the section hears their crime against the she-camel.
Thamud live among crops and tender date-palm spathes; the thriving palm makes their act of aqr, also used for cutting a palm's crown, especially pointed.
Gardens with rivers beneath are declared the reward of one who tazakka, joining purification-growth to the fully watered field exactly as the section does.
Even stone can split so rivers burst from it, while the addressed hearts are harder; the section's opened watercourse becomes a test of whether the inner ground can yield.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ restates both key terms of 91:9, making success and purification/growth an explicit pair.
Allah makes Mary grow with a beautiful growth and entrusts her to care, a direct human instance of the section's divinely nurtured plant-soul.
A spent grain grows seven ears with a hundred grains each, giving the spending context of 2:264-265 its positive image of blessed multiplication.
Earth is made a bed, sky a canopy, and water descends to bring fruit; this is the section's house becoming a field, with a watered ceiling and productive floor.
The divine question directs attention to what people till, isolating the human act of cleaving the soil that the section finds in falaha.
The question whether people make the crop grow or Allah does states the section's distinction between human ploughing and growth granted by divine blessing.
The command to consider the water people drink begins the second half of the same field lesson: the cultivator does not originate the field's water.
The question whether people bring water from the raincloud or Allah does directly matches the section's sama as cloud and rain that nurtures growth.
Abundant pouring water descends from rainclouds, repeating the section's image of water coming through the field's ceiling.
Grain and vegetation are brought out by that poured water, a compact parallel to the Abasa sequence of water, split soil, and growth.
Dense gardens complete the rain-to-growth sequence and show the mature abundance toward which the section's tarbiya proceeds.
Lifeless, barren earth stirs, swells, and grows every lovely kind after rain; it precisely crosses the section's boundary between sterile ground and living field.
Water from the sky is conducted as springs through the earth and produces varied crops, directly joining watercourses, irrigation, and growth before the crop withers.
Adjacent plots, vines, crops, and palms receive the same water yet differ in fruit, sharpening the section's claim that water alone does not make every inner ground alike.
Water from the sky brings green growth, grain, palms, and gardens, and the command to watch fruit ripen displays nurture from emergence to completion.
Dead earth is revived and grain is brought from it for people to eat, an exact reversal of the section's sand that grows nothing.
Palm and grape gardens are furnished with bursting springs, joining the section's fajara water-opening to productive land.
People eat the field's fruit though their hands did not create it, reinforcing the section's attribution of growth to the Lord's blessing.
Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and harvested grain, directly uniting sama, blessing, and crop growth.
Lofty palms with layered fruit clusters give the mature palm image whose growing point the section says aqr can destroy.
The crop is provision and the rain revives dead land, making the fertile/barren contrast also an image of human emergence.
Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, with an explicit warning that it can be removed; this clarifies the field's allotted drink and its dependence.
That measured water produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit, the mature outcome of the section's apportioned irrigation.
The gates of the sky open with pouring water; this reverses the nurturing ceiling-water image into the flood that destroys.
Earth is made to burst into springs and the two waters meet for a decreed matter, turning the section's opened irrigation channels into an overwhelming judgment.
Twelve springs burst from the struck stone and every people knows its drinking place, combining fajara-like opening with an apportioned share of water.
Twelve springs issue from the rock and each tribe knows its drinking place, a direct communal parallel to the she-camel's protected water share.
Salih states that the she-camel has one drink and the people another on an appointed day, explicitly spelling out the suqya whose violation 91 recalls.
The water is declared divided between Thamud and the she-camel, with each turn attended; it is the clearest parallel for the section's field-water allotment.
Thamud hamstring the she-camel and defy their messenger, preserving the exact aqr act whose secondary sense is cutting away the palm's growing crown.
After Thamud hamstring her, Salih gives them three days; this parallel keeps the aqr act inside the land-cultivation address of 11:61.
Thamud hamstring the camel and then regret it, repeating the section's action of cutting off life in a people surrounded by crops and palms.
They summon their companion, who takes hold and hamstrings the camel; the compact scene directly preserves the root عقر.
Zechariah calls his wife عَاقِر, barren; the human use illuminates the section's lexicon of aqir sand as ground from which no life emerges.
Zechariah's wife is again called barren, making عَاقِر a direct reproductive counterpart to the section's sterile sand.
The repeated description of the wife as عَاقِر reinforces the root's boundary between capacity for growth and apparent incapacity.
Believers are likened to a crop whose shoot emerges, strengthens, thickens, and stands on its stem, a full moral enactment of gradual plant-like nurture.
A good word is a good tree with a firm root and branches in the sky, giving the section's rooted, upward growth a moral form.
The good tree gives fruit continually by its Lord's permission, joining mature yield to the same divine permission named for good soil in 7:58.
The earth is spread out and every well-balanced thing is made to grow in it, directly pairing the section's spread ground with measured fertility.
Fertilizing winds are sent and water descends from the sky for people to drink, while they do not store its source; the field's growth and water remain divine provision.
Earth is made a bed, paths opened, water sent from the sky, and diverse plants brought forth, nearly reproducing the section's entire house-field sequence.
Water is driven to barren land and crops emerge for livestock and people, directly showing sterile ground made productive by routed water.
Humbled, lifeless earth stirs and swells when water descends, a precise revival of the section's non-growing ground.
The Lord brings out pasture, showing Rabb as the one who causes vegetation to emerge and begins its measured nurture.
Rain mingles with earth's plants until the land is adorned, then the crop is suddenly made as if harvested; growth and its removal expose the field's dependence.
The parable's two grape gardens, palms, and intervening crop present a deliberately ordered, productive field.
Both gardens yield fully and a river is made to gush between them, directly combining complete fruiting with the section's opened watercourse.
Saba's two gardens and command to eat their Lord's provision stage fertile land as a sign requiring gratitude.
Water descends from the sky for drink and for vegetation on which animals graze, matching sama as rain and plant-provider.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, expanding the section's green floor into its full produce.
Winds announce mercy and pure water descends from the sky, presenting the nourishing cloud-water aspect of sama.
That water revives dead land and waters livestock and people, joining land's life with the distribution of drink.
The question who sends rain and grows splendid gardens answers the section's agricultural acts by locating growth with Allah.
Water from the sky causes every noble kind to grow in earth, directly joining the spread land to divinely supplied fertility.
Winds raise cloud, which is driven to dead land and revives it; the named cloud performs the nurturing work the section hears in Rabb.
Measured water descends from the sky and revives a dead land, combining the field's allotted water with its passage from barrenness to growth.
Earth is spread out and then furnished for life, directly recalling the section's spread ground as the surface of a field.
Water and pasture are brought out from that spread earth, making the surface productive in the same sequence the section develops.
Noah promises abundant rain from the sky, supplying the water for the human-plant image later stated in 71:17.
That rain is joined to gardens and rivers as divine increase, linking human multiplication with the growth of a watered field.
Salih presents Allah's she-camel as a sign, lets her graze in Allah's earth, and forbids harm; this states the living boundary violated by aqr.
Salih tells Thamud to let Allah's camel feed in His earth and not harm her, joining the cultivated earth of 11:61 to the act later called aqr.
The ashamed father considers pushing the girl into the dust, the Quranic yedussuhu scene that the section uses for burial too deep for growth.
The bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, the moral reverse of a soul that takes root and multiplies like the section's fertile plant.
The cow is described as neither trained to plough the earth nor water the field, a Quranic boundary image for the two human acts central to the section's cultivated ground.
The corrupter destroys crop and offspring, making moral corruption visible as the ruin of precisely what the section's purification-field should grow.
A fruitful, watered palm-and-grape garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind, completing the spending parables with cultivated abundance suddenly made fruitless.
A freezing wind strikes and destroys the crop of people who wronged themselves, projecting inner wrongdoing as the loss of a field's growth.
A calamity from the sky can turn the proud garden into bare, slippery ground, reversing the section's rain-from-above into exposed infertility.
The garden's water may sink beyond recovery, defining the boundary of cultivation when its hidden watercourse is withdrawn.
The garden's fruit is encompassed and its trellises collapse, showing the completed crop undone when its owner mistakes gifted growth for possession.
After Saba turns away, the flood replaces their two gardens with bitter fruit, tamarisk, and sparse lote trees; managed fertility becomes meagre growth.
Allah could make the crop broken debris, setting the barren possibility beside the claim in 56:64 that He is its true grower.
The cultivators would be left lamenting their loss, exposing human labour's inability to secure growth.
Allah could make rainwater bitter, marking the boundary between water's mere presence and its fitness to nourish a field.
Rain-fed vegetation delights its cultivators, then yellows and becomes debris; the field renders visible growth that does not remain.
If water sinks away, no one can bring flowing water; the question exposes how quickly an irrigable field can become the section's sterile ground.
The pasture the Lord brings out becomes dark stubble, bounding the image of growth with its withering end.
The owners of a garden are tested when they swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a parable of presumed control over cultivated yield.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden at night while its owners sleep, locating the field's fate beyond their labour.
By morning the garden is like a field already stripped bare, the sudden sterile reverse of growth expected for harvest.
The command that the human look at his food frames 80:25-32 as a lesson in how a field's nourishment is made, not merely a list of crops.
Grapes and herbage continue the produce emerging from the split ground, showing the variety hidden in the section's single verb of growth.
Olives and palms extend the field sequence to trees, including the palm whose crown the section's secondary sense of aqr can cut away.
Dense gardens show the mature enclosure formed by water, split earth, and growth in the preceding ayat.
Fruit and pasture identify the yield of the cultivated earth for both human food and grazing.
The produce is provision for people and livestock, completing the field image as divinely apportioned sustenance.
Before the good-and-bad soil comparison, heavy clouds carry rain to dead land and bring fruit; it supplies the watering scene whose different receptions 7:58 explains.
The believer who does righteous deeds receives the highest ranks; this identifies the cultivated moral life whose watered-garden reward 20:76 names.
Charity is taken to cleanse and cause people to grow, linking the section's zakkaha to giving just as the rain-garden parables of 2:261-265 do.
The giver spends wealth seeking to purify or increase himself, preserving the section's link between expenditure and the growing soul.
Allah purifies whom He wills, supplying the theological limit to the field image: the soul's growth, like the crop's, depends on divine action.
Whoever purifies does so for his own soul, making the section's cultivation reflexive: the yield returns to the ground being cultivated.
Humans are known from their emergence from earth and are told not to declare themselves pure, joining earthen origin to a warning against claiming one's own growth.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, an invitation to the growth that the section sets against the buried and barren soul.
The possibility that the blind seeker may purify himself treats moral reception as growth, resonating with the later field sequence in the same surah.
The prayer recalls parents raising the child when small; this is the Quranic human instance of tarbiya as bringing something stage by stage toward maturity.
Pharaoh claims to have raised Moses as a child; his boast supplies a contrary human claim to the nurturing action that the section locates in Rabb.
After people are grown from earth like plants, they are returned into it and brought out again, distinguishing fruitful burial from the section's suffocating dassa.
Allah knows every grain in the darknesses of the earth, illuminating the hidden seed-state from which the section distinguishes burial that prevents emergence.
Allah splits grain and seed and brings living from dead, a non-irrigation formulation of the same opened-earth passage into growth.
Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure; the measured watercourses concretize the section's hillside channels and apportioned irrigation.
Every created provision has known measure and descends only in measure, clarifying why the field's water is a share rather than an owned source.
Water from the sky brings fruit and rivers are subjected, joining rain, produce, and running channels within one provision scene.
Rain revives earth after death and the cloud is held between sky and earth, giving both cloud and water the life-producing role developed for sama.
Rain revives earth after its death, a concise recurring formulation of the passage from non-growing ground to living soil.
Rain from the sky revives dead earth, restating the section's fertile/barren boundary as an acknowledged act of Allah.
Rain descends and revives earth after death, while lightning holds fear and hope; water can be awaited as the field's uncertain life.
Winds raise and spread cloud, then rain is seen emerging, detailing how the section's sky-cloud supplies water to earth.
The hearer is told to look at the traces of mercy in earth revived after death, turning the watered field into a sign of restored life.
Water from the sky produces fruits of differing colours, adding visible variety to the section's single principle of blessed growth.
Provision descends from the sky and revives earth after death, using the rain-fed field as a sign for those who reason.
Allah's reviving of earth after its death is offered as a clarified sign, supporting the section's moral use of fertile and dead ground.
A stream is placed below Mary beside the palm, bringing water to the place where fruit will be received.
Shaking the palm brings fresh ripe dates down, a compact scene of mature palm yield supported by the nearby stream.
Joseph commands seven years of diligent sowing and preservation of grain in its ears, presenting cultivation as foresighted care rather than guaranteed abundance.
Seven severe years consume what was stored, placing a long barren interval against the preceding years of crop growth.
A year of rain and pressing produce ends the drought, showing restored water returning a community to yield.
Faith and reverence would have opened blessings from sky and earth, while denial brings seizure; moral condition is expressed through the field's two sources.
The one seeking the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase in that harvest, while the worldly harvest is limited; cultivation becomes a measure of what the soul grows toward.
The ruined gardens are named repayment for ingratitude, explaining why the fertile land of 34:15 becomes poor growth in 34:16.
Water and pasture are expressly provision for people and livestock, completing the spread-earth scene as sustenance.
All living things are made from water after heaven and earth are parted; this supplies the cosmic premise beneath the section's water-enabled growth.
Allah spreads the earth, places rivers in it, and makes fruits, bringing the section's spread surface and cleaving waterways into one productive landscape.
Salih's prohibition against harming the she-camel marks the boundary immediately before Thamud perform aqr in 26:157.
The she-camel is sent as a trial and the prophet is told to watch patiently, introducing the apportioned-water command of 54:28 and the aqr of 54:29.
Abraham's wife calls herself barren with عَقِيم, a different root whose infertility still parallels the section's secondary image of sand incapable of producing life.
